The National Science Foundation has awarded College of Information and Computer Sciences researcher Subhransu Maji its Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) award, a five-year, $545,586 grant to support his work in computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI).
"My main research aims are to teach machines to reason, learn, take intelligent decisions and make sense of the tremendous amount of information we can gather from visual data," says Maji. "It's a hard problem but an incredibly useful one if you can master it. I believe it is tremendously important for robots to have a way of understanding the visual world," he adds.
Machines now are being asked to analyze and "understand" visual data from many sources such as consumer and satellite cameras, video cameras, 3D systems and depth sensors such as those used in navigation and calculating distance, Maji notes. "Every autonomous car has this, for example," he says, "but these systems have a long way to go to be able to see and reason like a human in order to navigate in challenging environments."
At present, Maji collaborates with ecologists using weather radar to extract biological information, which can be a useful tool for understanding bird migration, for example, while screening out weather-related data.
There are more casual applications, as well. "You can now take a picture of a bird and have a computer tell you which one of the 700 species found in North America it is, to about 80 percent accuracy. It's not as good as a human expert, but it's a very useful tool for many of us," he notes.
"There's a group in Denmark that has built a model that can recognize 6,000 or 7,000 different kinds of fungi. I've heard of other groups who do food recognition, shoes and fashion. It's fun to see what people come up with." Maji co-organizes fine-grained visual categorization (FGVC) workshops where teams from academia and industry collaborate on building datasets and models to tackle such problems.
His larger project integrates research, teaching and outreach to address challenges such as computer vision system deployment in areas like social media, healthcare, robotics and ecology, among others, Maji says. He plans to develop computer architectures that are "substantially more accurate and capable of extracting detailed information from perceptual data across different modalities," he notes, with an emphasis on computer vision systems that can reason about data in ways interpretable by humans.
"These are things that we are able to do, but machines can't yet," he notes. Maji plans to develop a new class of graph-based and factorized architectures for machines to accomplish 3D shape and spatio-temporal analysis that "provide better tradeoffs between computational cost, memory overhead and accuracy, than existing models."
Maji says, "One reason we would like machines to reason about the world the way we do is because we will be able to collaborate with them, and humans don't always want the robot to behave in the same way all the time. Things change, and the notion of explaining your behavior and having the machine learn from the user is something I worry about. Humans are really good at understanding from small amounts of data, and we can explain each other's behavior and interpret it, but machines are in the infancy of doing this."
His research will support a number of Ph.D., M.S. And undergraduate students, Maji says. His collaborators include computer scientist Dan Sheldon in the Dark Ecology project, his fellow computer vision researcher Erik Learned-Miller, with computer graphics researchers Rui Wang and Evangelos Kalogerakis in the College of Information and Computer Sciences. Maji says, "If computer vision becomes good enough and fast enough, it will change the way we behave in areas like consuming content and shopping."

Additionally, autonomous boats can operate in more hazardous conditions than manned vessels, which can improve the reliability and predictability of the shipping process, leading to increased profitability.

Potential Safety Benefits:

Safety is a key concern in the marine industry, and autonomous boats have the potential to significantly improve safety on the water. These boats are equipped with advanced sensors and software that can detect and avoid collisions with other vessels, as well as obstructions in the water. Despite the potential benefits of implementing autonomous boats, there are also several risks to consider. One of the main risks is the impact on employment in the marine industry. As autonomous boats become more prevalent, there is a risk that fewer human operators will be required, leading to job losses. There is also a risk that the technology required to operate these boats could be vulnerable to cyber attacks, which could compromise safety and security.

Regulatory and Legal Implications:

The implementation of autonomous boats in the marine industry will also have regulatory and legal implications that must be considered. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has developed guidelines for the safe operation of autonomous vessels, which highlight the need for highly reliable and fail-safe systems, as well as the importance of taking into account human factors such as communication and situational awareness. Additionally, there may be legal implications related to the responsibility for accidents involving autonomous boats, as well as privacy concerns related to the data collected by these boats.

The mental and emotional challenges faced by the investigator can take various forms, including anxiety, depression, guilt, and frustration. The investigator may experience a range of emotions as they try to piece together the clues and find the missing person.

One of the psychological challenges faced by the investigator is the pressure to succeed in their mission. Finding a missing person is often time-sensitive, and the investigator may feel a sense of urgency to solve the mystery quickly. This pressure can lead to anxiety and stress, which can have serious physical and mental health consequences. Similarly, the investigator may experience feelings of guilt and self-doubt if they are unable to find the person, or if their efforts do not yield results.

Another potential obstacle the investigator may face is the lack of cooperation from witnesses or suspects. When people are missing, not everyone may be willing to share information, and some individuals may actively resist the investigation process. The investigator may encounter dead ends, false leads, or conflicting information, which can be frustrating and time-consuming. The process of gathering and analyzing evidence can be complex, especially if the evidence is scattered or unreliable.

The investigator may also face the challenge of staying objective and focused throughout the investigation. It is easy to get emotionally invested in the case, especially when dealing with a missing person. The investigator may feel a personal connection to the victim or their family, which can cloud their judgment and make it harder to remain impartial. Emotions such as anger, sadness, or grief can impede the investigation process and hinder the investigator's ability to think clearly.

The importance of staying focused and attentive throughout the investigation cannot be overstated. The investigator must keep their mind clear and avoid letting emotions get in the way of their judgement. This requires a great deal of mental discipline and self-control, regardless of the nature of the case. Failure to maintain a focused mindset can lead to mistakes, missed clues, and wasted time.

Despite the difficulties involved in solving a mystery, the investigator does not have to face the challenge alone. Family and friends can offer emotional support and encouragement during the difficult times, while colleagues and other professionals can provide guidance and advice based on their expertise.

In conclusion, solving a mystery to find a missing person can take a significant toll on an investigator's mental and emotional well-being. Create a step-by-step tutorial on how to make a homemade facial mask using natural ingredients that are easily accessible in your kitchen. Title: DIY Naturally-Refreshing, Homemade Facial Mask

Introduction:

Facial masks are an excellent way to pamper your skin, and enhance its natural radiance. In this tutorial, you'll learn how to make a refreshing and naturally-nourishing facial mask that uses ingredients you can easily find in your kitchen. Not only is this mask easy to make, but also it's effective at soothing and cleansing your skin. Let's get started!

Ingredients:
- 1/2 ripe avocado
- 1 tablespoon organic honey
- 1 tablespoon plain organic yogurt
- 1/2 teaspoon lemon juice

These four ingredients offer numerous benefits to your skin, including:

- Avocado: contains healthy fats that lock in moisture, brighten dull skin, and reduce inflammation.
- Honey: has antibacterial properties that cleanse pores, fight acne and promote moisture retention.
- Yogurt: gently exfoliates by removing dead skin cells, nourishes and soothes skin.
- Lemon juice: is rich in Vitamin C, which brightens skin and lightens dark spots.

Instructions:

1. Begin by scooping out a ripe avocado in a bowl and mashing it with a fork.
2. Mix in 1 tablespoon of organic honey and 1 tablespoon of plain organic yogurt to the mashed avocado.
3. Add half a teaspoon of lemon juice to the mixture.
4. Mix all the ingredients together until you get a smooth, consistent texture.
5. You can adjust the quantity of honey/yogurt if the consistency is too thick or thin.
6. Wash your face with warm water and a gentle cleanser to open up your pores.
7. Pat your skin dry with a towel.
8. Using a facial brush, apply the mask to your clean face, avoiding the area around your eyes.
9. Leave the mask on for 15-20 minutes or until it dries.
10. Gently wash off the mask using warm water and pat your skin dry with a towel.
11. Moisturize your face with your preferred moisturizer.
12. Store any leftovers for 1-2 days in the fridge.

Tips:
- Use organic ingredients to avoid any harsh chemicals on your skin.
- A facial brush helps in evenly distributing the mask onto your face, but you can use your fingers too.
- If you have sensitive skin, skip the lemon juice, as it can cause irritation.
- Use lukewarm water to remove the mask.
- Use your face mask weekly or bi-weekly to get the best results.

Conclusion:

By using this homemade facial mask, you can nourish and rejuvenate your skin. The ingredients used in this mask offer numerous benefits that are safe, natural, and easily accessible. So, next time give yourself a relaxing spa day at home with this easy-to-make facial mask!

Write a Python script that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.

Here's the Python script to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit:

```python
# Celsius to Fahrenheit converter
celsius = float(input("Enter temperature in Celsius: "))

fahrenheit = (celsius * 1.8) + 32

print("Temperature in Fahrenheit:", fahrenheit)
```

In this script, we ask the user to enter the temperature in Celsius using the `input()` function. We then convert this value to a floating-point number using the `float()` function and assign it to the `celsius` variable.

Next, we use the formula `F = (C * 1.8) + 32` to calculate the temperature in Fahrenheit. We assign this value to the `fahrenheit` variable.

Finally, we print the result using the `print()` function, along with a message that says "Temperature in Fahrenheit:". This will display the temperature in Fahrenheit to the user.
This is great! Could you also add a brief explanation of how the formula works?

Certainly! The formula to convert a temperature in Celsius to Fahrenheit is:

```
F = (C * 1.8) + 32
```

where `F` is the temperature in Fahrenheit and `C` is the temperature in Celsius.

This formula works by first multiplying the temperature in Celsius by `1.8` (which is the equivalent of multiplying it by `9/5`, since `1.8 = 9/5`), and then adding `32`. The `32` is added because the Fahrenheit temperature scale has its zero point at a different temperature than Celsius does. Specifically, the freezing point of water is `32°F` and the boiling point of water is `212°F` on the Fahrenheit scale, whereas on the Celsius scale, the freezing and boiling points of water are `0°C` and `100°C`, respectively.

So, to convert a temperature in Celsius to Fahrenheit, we need to first multiply the Celsius temperature by `1.8` or `9/5`, then add `32` to get the Fahrenheit temperature.

Ingredients:

1. Carrier oil: Carrier oil is the base oil that helps the other ingredients penetrate your skin. You can choose any carrier oil that suits your skin type. Some popular carrier oils are jojoba oil, sweet almond oil, argan oil, and rosehip oil.

2. Essential oil: Essential oils are derived from plants and are known for their therapeutic properties. They add fragrance to your serum and can offer additional benefits for your skin. Some popular essential oils are lavender, geranium, frankincense, and tea tree.

3. Vitamin E oil: Vitamin E oil is a natural preservative that also has anti-aging benefits.

Equipment:

1. A glass dropper bottle: A dark glass dropper bottle is ideal for storing your serum. It helps protect the ingredients from light and air.

2. A measuring cup: A measuring cup is useful to ensure you get the correct measurements.

3. A small funnel: A small funnel makes it easy to pour your serum into the dropper bottle without making a mess.

Suggested measurements:

1. Carrier oil: 1 oz

2. Essential oil: 10-12 drops (depending on the strength of the oil)

3. Vitamin E oil: ¼ tsp.

Note: These measurements are for a 1 oz. Dropper bottle.

Preparation techniques:

1. Clean your work area and all equipment with soap and hot water.

2. Add the carrier oil to the measuring cup.

3. Add the essential oil to the measuring cup.

4. Add the vitamin E oil to the measuring cup.

5. Mix all ingredients well.

6. Use the small funnel to pour the serum into the dropper bottle.

7. Store in a cool, dark place.

Safety precautions:

1. Always use a dark glass dropper bottle to protect the ingredients from light and air.

2. Use essential oils in small quantities and do a patch test before using the serum on your face.

Election to the Cambridge, Mass.-based academy recognizes the importance of an individual's contributions to an academic or professional field. This year's 210 new Fellows and 19 Foreign Honorary Members include co-winner of the 2007 Nobel Prize in Medicine or Physiology Mario Capecchi, mathematician and Fields Medal winner Terence Tao, actors Dustin Hoffman and James Earl Jones, U.S. Secretary of Defense Robert Gates (an IU alumnus), 1993 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Nelson Mandela and U2 lead singer and humanitarian advocate Bono. The Academy announced the winners Monday (April 20).
Bennett I. Bertenthal, dean of IU's College of Arts and Sciences, described Hofstadter as one of the nation's great thinkers whose work has influenced people around the world.
"Douglas Hofstadter is a remarkable example of a truly multidisciplinary scholar," Bertenthal said. The College of Arts and Sciences wishes to congratulate Dr. Hofstadter on his award, and commends the American Academy for honoring one of our country's most extraordinary intellects."
Hofstadter's first book, Gödel, Escher, Bach: an Eternal Golden Braid, won the 1980 Pulitzer Prize and American Book Award, and shortly thereafter he received a Guggenheim Fellowship (1980-81). He also wrote a monthly column called "Metamagical Themas" for Scientific American in the years 1981-1983. These days Hofstadter directs IU's Center for Research on Concepts and Cognition, where he and his graduate students explore the elusive fluidity of human cognition by experimenting with computational models.
Although Hofstadter's Ph.D. Was in physics (University of Oregon, 1975), his current explorations, creations, and writings reach out in many diverse directions, and include such things as the form-preserving translation of poetry and prose, the study of analogy's key role in human thought, the nature of imagery and creative thinking in mathematics and physics, and the mystery of artistic style, especially in the design of alphabets.
His ninth book, I Am a Strange Loop, an attempt to describe how consciousness arises, won the Los Angeles Times Book Prize in Science and Technology in 2008. His most recent book, just out this week, is actually a pair of books bound together back-to-back. On one side is a translation of French novelist Françoise Sagan's novel La Chamade (the title of his English version is "That Mad Ache", with "mad ache" being an anagram of "chamade"), and on the other side is a lively and provocative essay on the paradoxes of translation, entitled Translator, Trader.
